headline: AI Agents can book trips, buy things, and send messages, but risk spending your money by mistake
summary: AI agents use LLMs, memory, tools, and rules to complete tasks autonomously. While powerful, weak guardrails or risky tool access can turn a small error into a real-world mistake, like accidental purchases.
details: Companies are rolling out AI agents that can book trips, buy things, and send messages for you. However, a single bad instruction can lead to unintended consequences, such as spending your money or emailing your boss by mistake.

AI agents are systems built around a large language model (LLM) that can work towards a goal across multiple steps. Unlike a plain LLM that gives one response, an agent can make a plan, take action, check results, and try again until a task is completed.

For example, a plain LLM might guess at flight prices or tell you to search yourself. An agent, however, can search travel sites, compare live prices, and return a curated list, demonstrating a shift towards system design over just model quality.

Most working agent systems share common building blocks. These include the LLM for flexible decision-making, memory for context and stored facts, and tools for external actions like web search, code execution, or payment systems.

Further components include state, which records what has happened, and planning, which breaks goals into actions. Crucially, guardrails limit what an agent can do (e.g., requiring approval for spending), and evaluation checks if actions were successful.

topic: big tech sues california over teen social media law
headline_marked: [[Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG]] over teen social media law
headline: Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law
summary: The tech giants are challenging a California law, AB 1709, which prohibits personalized feeds and autoplay videos for users under 16, set to take effect at the start of the new year.
details: Meta, Google, and TikTok have each filed lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta. They aim to block a new law, AB 1709, that restricts social media features deemed addictive for users under 16.

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1709 into law in September, and it is slated to take effect at the start of the new year. The law prohibits personalized feeds and autoplay videos for minors.
Platforms must delete accounts of users under 16 if they do not turn off these features. Non-compliance could lead to fines of up to $50,000 per affected user.

Meta, TikTok, and Google argue that AB 1709 violates the First Amendment by overriding their editorial decisions on content display. They claim it would make disseminating speech to minors unlawful without changing core practices.

Digital safety experts caution that such laws can inadvertently compromise the privacy of all users, including adults. They often require age verification checks that collect more user data, increasing online surveillance.

Critics also argue that AB 1709 could cut off young people from essential information and experiences, potentially silencing voices that have been instrumental in digital activism. Google highlights its existing parental controls and default settings for minors.

This legal battle is part of a global trend of legislation curbing teen social media use. Australia has banned social media for under-16s, while a similar French law was struck down over free expression concerns.
